angle: The best outbound plays aren't the templated ones. They're the weird, nuanced ones.
post_first_line: The weirdest use cases are often the best.
linkedin_post:
The weirdest use cases are often the best.

Skyler Mickunas says the most successful customer plays are often the most nuanced ones, not the templated ones.

Take Delve, a partner that has seen a lot of success. Delve wants to know if a target account is already SOC 2 compliant.

That isn't an out-of-the-box signal everyone in the audience will find valuable. It's specific to one business.

That's why Unify doesn't have a full set of templated use cases. It would be a lot of work for Ethan, and not all of them would be widely applicable for the average user.

Custom signals are a bit of a black box once you open it up.

The takeaway: the signal that matters most to your pipeline may not be one anyone else would think to track.

What's the most unusual signal you track?

A signal like SOC 2 compliance status is valuable to one business but not to everyone.
Templates can't cover every use case, since many aren't widely applicable to the average user.
lesson.exercise: Write down one question about a target account that only your business cares about, then work out how to turn it into a custom signal.

caption: Weird signals win

angle: We track about 100 signals, but the rep decides what to do with each one
post_first_line: We track close to 100 signals. Each one routes to a rep.
linkedin_post:
We track close to 100 signals. Each one routes to a rep.

The interesting part is what happens after the signal fires.

When a company hits one of those signals, we don't force a single playbook. The rep chooses the path.

Some reps want an auto email, with phone call tasks and LinkedIn tasks layered in so they can work out of Unify.

Some want a manual email where we hand over all the context, so they can write something specific as a sniper shot.

Some just want different alerts.

Whatever workflow the rep wants, we work backwards from that.

The goal is to maximize our share on each prospect and account.

Signals tell you when to act. The rep still decides how.

How much control do your reps have over signal response?

Slide 2: Every signal gets routed to a rep
Slide 3: The rep chooses the path, not the system
Slide 4: Option one: auto email plus phone and LinkedIn tasks
Slide 5: Option two: manual email with full context, a sniper shot
Slide 6: Option three: different alerts for the rep
Slide 7: We work backwards from the rep's desired workflow

lesson.title: Let reps choose the response to each signal
takeaways: Routing signals to reps is step one; the response should fit how each rep works.
Offer a range: auto email with added call and LinkedIn tasks, manual email with context, or alerts.
Work backwards from the rep's desired workflow to maximize share on each prospect and account.
lesson.exercise: Pick your top 5 signals. For each, write down the response paths a rep could take (auto, manual, alert only), then ask your reps which they would choose and why.

caption: 100 signals, rep decides

angle: Our rule: if a rep owns the account, it never goes into an automated play
post_first_line: 200 accounts per AE, 500 to 600 per MBR.
linkedin_post:
200 accounts per AE, 500 to 600 per MBR.

The rule that sits on top of those numbers is the one that matters most.

Here's how we split ownership: each account executive owns around 200 accounts. Each MBR owns around 500 to 600. We also have shared accounts by segment, and an inbound MBR who handles our warmer, inbound-driven signals.

The automated plays run outside all of that. They go after signals where an account might be a good fit for Unify.

One rule beats everything else in our setup: account ownership trumps all.

If Audrey, an MBR on our team, owns an account, we don't funnel it into an automated play. We route Audrey the signal instead. Audrey decides what to do with it based on how Audrey likes to work.

Automation should fill the gaps reps don't cover. It shouldn't step on accounts they own.

How do you handle rep-owned accounts in automation?

Slide 2: Each MBR owns around 500 to 600 accounts.

Slide 4: Automated plays run outside all of those owned accounts.
Slide 5: Our rule: account ownership trumps all.
Slide 6: Rep owns it? It never enters an automated play.
Slide 7: The rep gets the signal and decides what to do.
Slide 8: Automation fills the gaps. Reps own the relationships.

lesson.title: Account ownership trumps automation
takeaways: Define clear account ownership by role before building any automated plays.
Run automation only on accounts no rep owns.
When a signal fires on an owned account, route it to the rep instead of an automated sequence.
lesson.exercise: Export your current automated plays and check how many target accounts a rep already owns. Pull those accounts out and set up a signal alert to the owner instead.

caption: Ownership trumps automation

angle: Why we tell our AEs not to automate their outreach
post_first_line: Skyler Mickunas tells AEs to skip automated outreach.
linkedin_post:
Skyler Mickunas tells AEs to skip automated outreach.

The reason has to do with who ends up doing the high-volume work instead.

According to Skyler Mickunas, AEs can run automated plays to pick up on signals, like new hires at target accounts. We encourage that. What we steer them away from is automating engagement itself.

AEs have a strong grasp of the value prop and of what different decision makers care about. That means they run a much lower volume of really high converting outreach.

Our AEs are closed lost circle back specialists. When a prospect says the timing is off, they set a reminder. Then a prospect mentions hiring a head of demand gen, and the AE knows that person would want a look.

If AEs started running automated email sequences, their time would be better spent on what we call sniper work. Automated sequences are something Ethan could replicate.

Signals can be automated. Judgment stays with the AE.

Where do you draw the line on automation?

Slide 2: Automating signals is encouraged. Automating engagement is not.

Slide 4: That means lower volume and higher converting outreach.

Slide 7: A new demand gen hire is their cue to reach out.
Slide 8: Automated sequences are replicable. Sniper work is the better use of time.

lesson.title: Automate the signal, not the conversation
takeaways: Automated plays that catch signals, like new hires at target accounts, are worth running.
AEs who know the value prop and each decision maker can run lower volume, higher converting outreach.
Circling back on closed lost deals when timing changes is work AEs do well.
lesson.exercise: List your AEs' outreach tasks and mark each as signal detection or engagement. Automate the signal tasks and keep the engagement ones manual.

caption: Don't automate your AEs

angle: Pushing reps from 300 to 1,000 accounts a week just makes conversion pay the price
post_first_line: Reps do their best work at 200 to 300 accounts weekly.
linkedin_post:
Reps do their best work at 200 to 300 accounts weekly.

Push past that and something quietly breaks.

Skyler Mickunas pointed out that it's naive to expect a rep to work 500 to 1,000 accounts per week as diligently as 200 to 300.

When volume expectations get too high, conversion on average activity pays the price.

And the goal is the outcome. If volume goes up and conversion goes down, the outcome probably doesn't move in any meaningful way.

So on the Unify team, reps work about 500 to 600 accounts per month diligently. That keeps enough tender loving care in each individual outbound effort.

The math will vary case by case. But the principle holds: more accounts touched is not the same as more pipeline created.

What's your rep's real account capacity?

Slide 4: Volume goes up. Conversion on average activity drops.
Slide 5: If conversion falls, the outcome barely moves.

Slide 7: That leaves real care in every outbound effort.
Slide 8: Your math will vary. Optimize for outcomes, not volume.

lesson.title: Account volume is not the goal. Outcomes are.
takeaways: Expecting reps to work 500 to 1,000 accounts per week as diligently as 200 to 300 is naive.
When volume pressure rises too high, conversion of average activity pays the price.
If volume rises while conversion falls, the outcome likely won't move much.
lesson.exercise: Pull your reps' accounts worked versus conversion rate for the last quarter. Find the volume level where conversion starts to drop, then set your account target just below it.

caption: More accounts, worse conversion

angle: What Ethan and I work together on is we've got 10,000 accounts.
post_first_line: 10,000 target accounts. Good coverage on about 6,000.
linkedin_post:
10,000 target accounts. Good coverage on about 6,000.

The gap between those two numbers is where most outbound teams quietly lose pipeline.

Skyler Mickunas works with Ethan on exactly this problem. Too much AI and automation, and the conversion rate pays the price. Too much manual effort, and a coverage gap opens up.

Skyler Mickunas put it plainly: everybody wants a fully automatic sniper rifle, but that does not exist.

So the two of them split the list. Ethan, on the growth and RevOps side, helps work out that not every account in the 10,000 is equally attractive. Together they identify the top half, the tier 1 and tier 2 accounts, where human attention goes.

Then they build automated coverage over everything else.

As human headcount scales, more of tier 1 and tier 2 can be worked by hand.

The point isn't choosing between automation and people. It's deciding which accounts earn which.

How do you split accounts between human and automated coverage?

Slide 2: Too much automation, and conversion rate pays the price.
Slide 3: Too much manual effort, and a coverage gap opens up.
Slide 4: A fully automatic sniper rifle does not exist.
Slide 5: Not every account on the list is equally attractive.
Slide 6: Humans take tier 1 and tier 2 accounts.
Slide 7: Automation covers everything else on the list.
Slide 8: Add headcount, and humans take on more of the top tiers.

lesson.title: Split your account list between humans and automation
takeaways: Too much automation hurts conversion; too much manual effort creates a coverage gap.
Not every target account is equally attractive, so tier the list.
Put human effort on tier 1 and tier 2, automate coverage on the rest, and shift as headcount grows.
lesson.exercise: Take your target account list and mark the top half as tier 1 and tier 2. Then write down which accounts get human outreach and which get automated coverage.
